scenes.visual: Title card 'A Region Outlasts Its Ponds' over the 20-pond map, about three quarters of the ponds TEAL. COLOUR MAP, same in both films and the lesson's figures: a fixed top-down map of 20 ponds on pale farmland; OCCUPIED pond = filled TEAL; EMPTY pond = GREY outline; colonization = GOLD arrow from an occupied pond to an empty one; local extinction = a teal pond fading to grey with a small RED tick; on graphs, gains = GOLD curve, losses = RED straight line; symbols on screen are always p (fraction occupied), c (colonization rate), e (extinction rate). Cream background, 16:9. Every number appears as on-screen text. Ponds and animals are simple cartoons; curves and map runs computed from the Levins model are labelled 'computed'; anything else is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: On this map, each pond's frogs last only about a decade. So why can the region still have frogs a century later?
scenes.visual: The 20-pond map. One TEAL pond is highlighted; a small clock beside it runs to '~10 years' and the pond fades to GREY with a RED tick. Then a larger clock reads '100 years' over the whole map, still partly TEAL. A question mark appears. Schematic.
scenes.narration: On this map, each pond's frogs last only about a decade. So why can the region still have frogs a century later?

scenes.tts: Each pond holds a local population, the frogs that live and breed there. The fields between are hostile ground. Ponds linked by dispersal like this form a metapopulation.
scenes.visual: Zoom into one TEAL pond with cartoon frogs, label 'local population'. Pull back: the fields between ponds turn a muted brown, label 'hostile ground'. Thin dashed GOLD lines briefly link ponds; a bracket around the whole map reads 'metapopulation'.
scenes.narration: Each pond holds a local population, the frogs that live and breed there. The fields between are hostile ground. Ponds linked by dispersal like this form a metapopulation.

scenes.tts: Richard Levins asked the question simply. Forget how many frogs a pond holds. Each pond is either occupied or empty. Then follow one number: the fraction of ponds occupied.
scenes.visual: Name card 'Richard Levins, 1969'. The frogs vanish from the map; each pond becomes a plain TEAL disc or GREY ring. A counter in the corner appears: 'p = fraction occupied = 15/20 = 0.75'.
scenes.narration: Richard Levins asked the question simply. Forget how many frogs a pond holds. Each pond is either occupied or empty. Then follow one number: the fraction of ponds occupied.

scenes.tts: Now let the map run. Ponds go grey as their populations die out. Others turn teal as colonists arrive. Which ponds are teal keeps changing, yet the teal fraction hovers near three quarters.
scenes.visual: The map runs forward year by year (computed, one random run with c = 0.4, e = 0.1 per year shown on screen). Ponds fade to GREY with RED ticks; GOLD arrows fly from TEAL ponds to GREY ones, which turn TEAL. The counter p flickers around 0.75 while a small line trace beside it wobbles about a dashed line at 0.75.
scenes.narration: Now let the map run. Ponds go grey as their populations die out. Others turn teal as colonists arrive. Which ponds are teal keeps changing, yet the teal fraction hovers near three quarters.

scenes.tts: Losses are the simple side of the ledger. Each occupied pond loses its population at a steady extinction rate. So total losses grow in a straight line with the fraction occupied.
scenes.visual: The map shrinks to the top-left corner. A graph builds: x axis 'p, fraction occupied' 0 to 1; y axis 'fraction of ponds per year'. A RED straight line rises from the origin, labelled 'losses = e p'. As the line draws, more ponds on the mini-map turn TEAL and more RED ticks appear.
scenes.narration: Losses are the simple side of the ledger. Each occupied pond loses its population at a steady extinction rate. So total losses grow in a straight line with the fraction occupied.

scenes.tts: Gains are different. Colonists must come from an occupied pond, and they can only found a population in an empty one. So gains need both kinds of pond.
scenes.visual: On the mini-map a GOLD arrow leaves a TEAL pond and lands on a GREY pond, which turns TEAL. Labels: 'from occupied: p' and 'to empty: 1 − p'. The formula 'gains = c p (1 − p)' appears in GOLD beside the graph.
scenes.narration: Gains are different. Colonists must come from an occupied pond, and they can only found a population in an empty one. So gains need both kinds of pond.

scenes.tts: With no ponds occupied, there are no colonists. With every pond occupied, there is nowhere to land. Between those two ends, gains rise and then fall in a hump.
scenes.visual: A GOLD curve draws on the same graph: zero at p = 0 (mini-map all GREY, no arrows), rising to a peak at p = 0.5, back to zero at p = 1 (mini-map all TEAL, arrows with nowhere to land bounce off). Computed, c = 0.4.
scenes.narration: With no ponds occupied, there are no colonists. With every pond occupied, there is nowhere to land. Between those two ends, gains rise and then fall in a hump.

scenes.tts: Where the gold hump meets the red line, gains equal losses. The occupied fraction settles there. That level is one minus the ratio of extinction to colonization. With these rates, it sits at three quarters.
scenes.caption: Where the gold hump meets the red line, gains equal losses. The occupied fraction settles there. That level is one minus the ratio of extinction to colonization, p* = 1 − e/c. With these rates, it sits at three quarters.
scenes.visual: A white dot marks where the GOLD hump crosses the RED line, labelled 'p* = 1 − e/c'. On-screen: 'c = 0.4, e = 0.1 per year', 'p* = 1 − 0.1/0.4 = 0.75'. Arrows on the x axis show p rising toward the dot from below (gains above losses) and falling toward it from above (losses above gains). Computed.
scenes.narration: Where the gold hump meets the red line, gains equal losses. The occupied fraction settles there. That level is one minus the ratio of extinction to colonization, p* = 1 − e/c. With these rates, it sits at three quarters.

scenes.tts: Now halve the colonization rate, and keep extinction the same. Does the occupied fraction halve too? Make your guess before the graph moves.
scenes.visual: On-screen: 'c: 0.4 → 0.2, e stays 0.1'. The GOLD hump is shown dashed, about to shrink; the white dot pulses with a question mark.
scenes.narration: Now halve the colonization rate, and keep extinction the same. Does the occupied fraction halve too? Make your guess before the graph moves.

scenes.visual: Graph frozen; a small countdown 5 to 1 in the corner.

scenes.tts: No. The hump shrinks, and the crossing slides only from three quarters to one half. What matters is the ratio of the two rates, not either one alone.
scenes.visual: The GOLD hump shrinks to half its height (computed, c = 0.2). The white dot slides left along the RED line from 0.75 to 0.50. On-screen: 'p* = 1 − 0.1/0.2 = 0.50'. On the mini-map the teal fraction drops to about half of the ponds.
scenes.narration: No. The hump shrinks, and the crossing slides only from three quarters to one half. What matters is the ratio of the two rates, not either one alone.

scenes.tts: Now push extinction up instead. The red line steepens, and the crossing slides left. When extinction equals colonization, the line only touches the hump at zero. No crossing above zero is left.
scenes.visual: Back to c = 0.4. A slider labelled 'e' moves from 0.1 to 0.4; the RED line steepens, the white dot slides left to 0 and disappears when e = c, where the line is tangent to the hump at the origin. On-screen: 'e = c → p* = 0'. Computed. Do not show any time course.
scenes.narration: Now push extinction up instead. The red line steepens, and the crossing slides left. When extinction equals colonization, the line only touches the hump at zero. No crossing above zero is left.

scenes.tts: So, in the model, a region keeps a species only while colonization beats extinction. No single pond has to last. Refounding balances loss at a level above zero.
scenes.visual: The graph returns to c = 0.4, e = 0.1 with the white dot at 0.75. Large text: 'c > e'. The mini-map grows back to full size and keeps winking: GOLD arrows refounding GREY ponds as others fade.
scenes.narration: So, in the model, a region keeps a species only while colonization beats extinction. No single pond has to last. Refounding balances loss at a level above zero.

scenes.tts: The model is deliberately simple. Its ponds are identical, all equally reachable, with rates that never change. Real networks have big and small, near and far ponds. And a small network can lose every pond by chance, even when colonization wins.
scenes.visual: Three small icons beside the map: identical discs, arrows from every pond to every other, and a flat rate line, each labelled 'model assumption'. Then the map morphs into a schematic real landscape with ponds of different sizes and spacing, labelled 'real networks: schematic'. Finally a tiny 5-pond map winks out completely, labelled 'small network: chance loss, even with c > e'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: The model is deliberately simple. Its ponds are identical, all equally reachable, with rates that never change. Real networks have big and small, near and far ponds. And a small network can lose every pond by chance, even when colonization wins.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line: 'A region keeps a species only while colonization beats extinction.'
